definition.text: Fisheries management is the set of tasks that guide users and managers toward the best use of renewable aquatic resources, mainly fish.

facts.text: Its goal is to produce lasting biological, environmental and socioeconomic benefits from renewable aquatic resources.
Wild fish stocks count as renewable when they produce a yearly surplus that careful management can harvest without lowering future productivity.
The FAO says there is no clear, generally accepted definition, and uses a working one covering information gathering, planning, decision-making, rule-making and enforcement.
Modern management is often a government system of rules based on set objectives, enforced through monitoring, control and surveillance.
Fisheries have been explicitly managed in some places for hundreds of years; Norway passed a law on the Lofoten fishery in 1816.
In Europe, government management to protect fish stocks began after the first Overfishing Conference in London in 1936.
A 2008 World Bank and FAO report put the economic loss from depleted stocks and poor management at US$50 billion a year.
Fisheries scientist Milo Adkison argues that the main limit on management decisions is the lack of good-quality data.

definition.text: In economics, the aim of fisheries management is to maximise the present value of all future profits from a fishery, which is treated as a common property resource.

facts.text: Economists often define fisheries as common property resources, which suffer the problems of open-access goods, chiefly overexploitation.
The problem was first analysed at length in H. Scott Gordon's 1954 article and Anthony D. Scott's 1955 article, both in the Journal of Political Economy.
Gordon showed that without intervention, fishers keep entering until total value minus costs is zero, so profits dissipate.
Both articles were foundational for environmental economics, giving the basic economic case for managing renewable resources.
A main remedy for this market failure is to assign property rights, which the broadest economic survey suggests prevents population collapse.
Newer models add differing technologies and costs among users, uncertainty and the biology of fish population growth.

definition.text: Fisheries regulation falls into four core categories that limit either what goes into fishing (inputs such as boats and gear) or what comes out (the catch), directly or indirectly.

facts.text: Indirect input control is vessel licensing; direct input control is limited entry.
Output controls are rules on catching techniques or equipment (indirect) and catch quotas with technical regulation (direct).
Technical measures include minimum mesh sizes, bans on certain nets or weapons, and limits on vessel numbers and time at sea.
Many countries run fisheries ministries that control fishing within their exclusive economic zones.

definition.text: Large, old female fish turn out to matter far more than young ones for keeping fisheries productive, contrary to traditional management.

facts.text: Traditional management thinned out old, slow-growing fish to leave room for younger, faster-growing ones.
Larvae from older mothers grow faster, resist starvation better and are much more likely to survive.
Ignoring older fish may help explain recent collapses of some major US West Coast fisheries; marine reserves let populations age naturally.

definition.text: Ecosystem-based fisheries management manages fishing for the health and productivity of the whole ecosystem rather than for single target species.

facts.text: Current scientific consensus favours it as the most workable way to balance human needs, keep ecosystem services and limit ecological harm.
Instead of focusing on one species, it is organised around ecosystem services.
A 2007 set of 'ten commandments' urged keeping big old females, natural stock boundaries, seafloor habitats and food-web links.
It also asks managers to adapt to climate change, account for fishing-driven evolution and include human social and economic systems.
Pitcher and Pauly argue that rebuilding ecosystems, not sustainability as such, should be the goal, since harvesting simplifies ecosystems toward small, low-level species.

definition.text: Ecopath with Ecosim is a software suite for modelling marine ecosystems, widely used in fisheries management.

facts.text: It began as a NOAA initiative and was later developed mainly at the University of British Columbia's Fisheries Centre.
In 2007 NOAA named it one of the ten biggest scientific breakthroughs in its 200-year history.
As of 2010 it had 6000 registered users in 155 countries.

definition.text: The BIDE model is the basic accounting rule of population dynamics: next period's numbers equal current numbers plus births and immigrants, minus deaths and emigrants.

facts.text: It is written N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E.
In wild fisheries, immigration and emigration happen but are usually not measured.
Over-simple models that ignored fish size, age, bycatch and habitat damage have sped the collapse of key stocks.

definition.text: A sustainable fishery is conventionally one harvested at a rate at which the fish population does not decline over time because of fishing.

facts.text: It combines theory such as population dynamics with practice: quotas, curbing illegal fishing, protected areas and certification.
Worries include lost yield, stocks losing diversity and resilience, boom-and-bust cycles and fishing down marine food webs.
Global wild fisheries are believed to have peaked and begun to decline.
Fisheries and aquaculture support the livelihoods of over 500 million people, mostly in developing countries.
Over 70% of fish species are fully exploited, overexploited, depleted or recovering from depletion.
A 2021 UN report said sustainable fisheries made up about 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017.

definition.text: There are three ways to define a sustainable fishery: long-term constant yield, preserving intergenerational equity, and maintaining a whole biological, social and economic system.

facts.text: Constant yield is called naive because marine stocks fluctuate naturally.
The widely accepted intergenerational view counts only damage needing more than one generation to rebuild as unsustainable.
The system view may accept losing some species if the ecosystem keeps its integrity and keeps delivering useful products.

definition.text: Overfishing in the traditional sense, catching so much that yield falls below what lighter fishing would give, is not automatically unsustainable.

facts.text: A salmon run kept at half its optimal spawning escapement can be fished indefinitely at lower yield.
Hilborn calls such overfishing a misallocation of society's resources rather than a conservation threat, but it can precede collapse.
Hilborn says persisting with fishing while stocks collapse is largely a product of institutional failure.

definition.text: Repeatedly dragging heavy bottom trawls and dredges over the seabed flattens its habitats and radically changes the communities living there.

facts.text: Nearly all continental shelves and large areas of slopes, ridges and seamounts have been trawled repeatedly.
For fifty years governments and bodies such as the Asian Development Bank encouraged building trawler fleets.
Mangrove loss of about 0.5 percent a year since the 2000s shrinks nursery habitat that over four million mangrove fishers rely on.

definition.text: In 1883 Thomas Huxley claimed overfishing was scientifically impossible and the great sea fisheries inexhaustible, even as fisheries were already collapsing.

facts.text: By then the Atlantic halibut fishery had already collapsed and never recovered.
The United States Fish Commission had been set up 12 years earlier to find out why New England fisheries were declining.
